item.title: AADS Brown Bag - Sick Work — Fri Oct 2, 11:00 AM — East Duke Parlors
item.description:
In Sick Work, Rogers shows the unpaid labor it takes to be recognized as sick in the United States. Through a historical and ethnographic account of myalgic encephalomyelitis / chronic fatigue syndrome (ME/CFS)-a disease defined by disproportionate exhaustion after any form of exertion, which has no cures or treatments-she reveals how changing formations of labor decide what counts as disability and what does not. Sickness, she writes, is not work's opposite. Rather, people with ME/CFS are forced to do their own labor of disease advocacy, or "sick work," even as their symptoms prevent many from working paid jobs. Examining the everyday lives of people with ME/CFS and their activist movements, Sick Workdemands a radical transformation of how work is defined and valued.
Source: Duke Arts, Duke University

item.title: How to Think About Risk from “Data Poor” Chemicals — Fri Oct 2, 12:00 PM — None
item.description: Most of the chemicals people encounter have never undergone formal safety testing. Traditional testing focuses on pharmaceuticals, food additives, and active ingredients in pesticides. Thousands of other chemicals are used in commerce and detected in the environment and in human blood. For these "data-poor" chemicals, new approach methods (NAMs) can provide initial estimates of risk-relevant properties. Both in silico, structure-based NAMs and in vitro NAMs can generate hazard predictions at scale. Complementary exposure NAMs rely on computational tools calibrated against biomonitoring data to estimate daily chemical intake rates. High-throughput toxicokinetics (HTTK) converts hazard NAM concentrations and doses into equivalent daily intake rates necessary to cause hazard. Comparing these two chemical intakes (hazard and exposure) allows for chemical prioritization based on the ratio of NAM-derived points of departure to estimated exposure intake rates. item.title: Flipping the Bird Friday — Fri Oct 2, 12:15 PM — Rubenstein Library Mary Duke Biddle Room
item.description:
Duke University Libraries will be turning the pages of the Birds of America on the first Friday of every month! We welcome you to stop by and watch-what bird will be next?
Birds of America is one of the greatest undertakings in the history of both art and ornithology. Almost 200 years after its publication, it remains a primary resource for scientists and scholars. This four-volume, double-elephant-folio edition on handmade paper measures three feet tall and two feet wide and comprises 435 hand-colored prints impressed from copperplate engravings. Of the original 175 to 200 complete sets, 125 have survived. Nine species of those depicted have since gone extinct.
Source: Duke University

item.title: Exchangeable random permutations for Bayesian graph matching — Fri Oct 2, 3:30 PM — None
item.description: We introduce a new theory of exchangeable random permutations by linking the cycle representation of permutations to the literature on exchangeable random partitions. A novel sequential metaphor, the position-aware Chinese restaurant process (PA-CRP), provides a constructive foundation for this theory and supports practical algorithmic design. As an application, we develop a Bayesian model for graph matching that combines the PA-CRP with a correlated stochastic block model likelihood by linking the cycle structure of the matching permutation to the latent node community memberships. Posterior inference is performed through a node-wise blocked Gibbs sampler directly inspired by the proposed sequential construction, allowing coherent updates in the complex permutation space. To summarize posterior uncertainty, we introduce perSALSO, an adaptation of the SALSO algorithm to the permutation domain that provides principled point estimation and interpretable posterior summaries. "Remake" (Ross McElwee, 2026, 116 min, USA, DCP)
Filmmaker Ross McElwee has spent forty years recording himself and his family, creating documentaries that chronicle the shifting contours of American society through the lens of personal history. His son Adrian grew up inside those films, and eventually began experimenting with the camera himself. When a Hollywood producer acquires the rights to adapt McElwee's 1986 breakthrough "Sherman's March" into a work of fiction, twenty-year-old Adrian sees a chance for his father to finally reach a wider audience. As the adaptation stalls, Adrian gets swept into a deepening drug addiction and dies from a fentanyl overdose, leaving behind hours of personal video footage. Retracing Adrian's final years, McElwee reckons with what his camera captured and what remained hauntingly out of frame. item.title: Duke Arts Presents: MAJOR — Fri Oct 2, 7:30 PM — Bryan Center Reynolds Industries Theater
item.description:
Six dancers take the stage in MAJOR to explore the power, memory, and physicality of majorette dance, a form that originated in the American South within Historically Black Colleges and Universities in the 1960s. In this dance-theater work, six Black femmes revisit the rhythms of their girlhood and rediscover the bodies they shaped through choreography, spoken word, and a music score by Lambkin blending Southern rap, horns, drumlines, and melodic R&B and soul.
The work is created by Brooklyn-based dance and interdisciplinary artist Ogemdi Ude, whose performances explore Black femme legacies, grief, and futures, grief, and memory through movement and voice. Ude describes MAJOR as "a nuanced love letter to the folks who taught the team how to be proudly Black and proudly femme."
Source: Duke University

item.title: AGS: Yorktown Staff Ride — Sat Oct 3, 8:00 AM — None
item.description:
On October 3 and 4, the Program in American Grand Strategy will hold our annual staff ride - this year to Yorktown, Virginia, site of the final major campaign of the American Revolutionary War.
2026 marks the 250th anniversary of American independence, and the Yorktown campaign of 1781 is the hinge on which that independence turned. Without Washington and Rochambeau's audacious march south, without the French fleet's decisive victory at the Battle of the Capes, and without the siege that forced Cornwallis's surrender, there might be no United States. There is no better moment to walk this ground.
A staff ride is a hands-on educational experience where participants walk the terrain of a battle or campaign. item.description:
Eight hundred years after his death, St. Francis of Assisi remains one of the most recognizable and beloved figures in Christian history. But the real Francis was far more interesting-and challenging-than the gentle saint surrounded by birds and animals that we often imagine.
Join Pastor Ryan for a conversation about Francis's remarkable life, his embrace of poverty and simplicity, his encounters across boundaries, his sense of kinship with all creation, and the movement he inspired. Along the way, we'll ask what this 13th-century saint might still have to teach the Church-and us-800 years later.

item.title: The Ritual of Belonging: 35 Years of the Friday Center — Thu Nov 5, 6:30 PM — William and Ida Friday Center
item.description:
Come. Connect. Celebrate.
In 1991, UNC President William C. Friday opened the doors to what he called "the citizens' classroom," a place built to make learning and connection open to everyone, with or without a UNC degree. Named for Bill and Ida Friday, two North Carolinians defined by their service to education and public life, the Friday Center was founded on a simple belief: learning never stops.
For 35 years, the Friday Center has carried that belief forward by opening doors, bringing people together, and extending Carolina's knowledge beyond the traditional classroom. It is a place where the University and the community meet, where ideas are shared, relationships are built, and learning becomes part of a larger public life.
This November, we're celebrating 35 years with an evening centered on something that has always been essential to the Friday Center: the power of gathering, and the belonging it creates.

item.title: Dec 10 - AI, ML and Computer Vision Meetup — Thu Dec 10, 12:00 PM
item.description:
Raleigh AI, Machine Learning and Computer Vision Meetup Join our virtual meetup to hear talks from experts on cutting-edge topics across AI, ML, and computer vision.
**Date, Time and Location**
Dec 10, 2026 9:00 AM - 11:00 AM PST Online. **[Register for the Zoom!](https://voxel51.com/events/ai-ml-and-computer-vision-meetup-december-10-2026)**
**Your mAP is fine. Your slices are not. Finding the images that actually matter**
A single mAP can look acceptable while one slice is unusable, small objects, occlusion, or a confused class. I will run a pretrained detector on a few hundred public images (COCO-style, not a production crawl), report the headline metric, then break the same run by slice and walk through the worst samples.
The claim is modest: you do not need a million images or a trained-from-scratch model to see what the mean is hiding, and you cannot relabel everything, so the next labeling budget should follow those slices. No employer data and no confidential dashboards.

item.title: Community Stories: Sustaining North Carolina’s Black Heritage — Wed Dec 30, 10:00 AM — Gregg Museum of Art & Design
item.description:
Community Stories: Sustaining North Carolina’s Black Heritage at the Gregg Museum of Art & Design presents a series of vignettes exploring spaces of dignity, belonging, safety, and imagination within Black communities across North Carolina. Featuring historical photographs, contemporary images, artworks from the Gregg Museum collection including a handmade guitar by Freeman Vines, and ephemera from community partners, the exhibition reflects on place, memory, creativity, and spiritual resilience across generations. Through stories of triumph and adversity, Community Stories honors the ways Black Americans have sustained and uplifted their communities through family, entrepreneurship, cultural expression, and soulful imagination, while inspiring future generations.
Source: NC Cultural Resources
